sm: Albert Mohler notes that Thanksgiving Day is tomorrow and that George Washington declared a national day of thanksgiving for November 26, 1789. He points out that only four nations, the United States, Canada, Liberia and St. Lucia, have a national Thanksgiving holiday, and that in each the thanks are given to God within a biblical background. He distinguishes harvest festivals, which appear across many agrarian cultures, from a day of thanksgiving, and says both reflect an impulse to thank someone. He then traces the holiday through the Reformation, when Protestants trimmed the crowded medieval church calendar, and the Puritans kept only special days of thanksgiving or humiliation.

He says the Pilgrims and Virginia colonists knew exactly whom they thanked, the triune God of the Bible. Today, he argues, secularization leaves millions of Americans feeling thankful with no idea to whom. He cites Richard Dawkins attending church services for the music and culture, and asks how anyone can be thankful to an impersonal cosmos or to the law of gravity. Mohler says people made in God's image have an urge to give thanks they cannot explain, and he sees thankfulness turning into a generalized sense of awe in poetry and landscape painting. He adds that Washington's proclamation was clearly theistic, in a country that was about 94 percent Protestant.

Mohler turns to Romans chapter 1, verses 18 through 25, where Paul says people suppress the truth in unrighteousness even though God has made himself plain in creation. He calls verse 21, that they knew God but did not honor him or give thanks, the hinge, and says the refusal to give thanks is the primal impulse of sin. He notes that Eastern Christianity tends to name lust as the basic sin, while the West names pride and ingratitude, which he links to Adam and Eve and original sin. Only God's grace and the gospel, he says, make true thankfulness possible. He closes by urging Christians to see Thanksgiving as a gracious opportunity for witness, to gather with thankful hearts, and wishes listeners a happy Thanksgiving.
